```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(cudaGlmnet)
```

## Why this vignette exists

`cudaGlmnet` fits the Gaussian lasso with a single FISTA solve executed by the
low-level `rcupp` package. This document has two independent goals:

1. **Numerical cross-check.** Compare our GPU coefficients against (a) the
   dependency-free pure-R oracle `lasso_fista_cpu()` and (b) a genuinely
   independent third-party GPU lasso, `cuda.ml::cuda_ml_lasso()` (RAPIDS cuML).
   A third implementation rules out the possibility that the oracle and the
   compiled path share the same mistake.
2. **Build-system notes.** Show that `rcupp`'s optional-CUDA `configure` follows
   the same pattern as `gputools` 2.1.0, and record how that pattern handles
   multiple platforms (Linux toolkit vs conda layouts, Windows/WSL2, per-GPU
   architecture).

The two parts are deliberately decoupled: Part 1 needs a working GPU stack,
Part 2 is pure documentation and always renders.

## Part 1 - Numerical cross-check

### Optional third-party backend

`cuda.ml` is in `Suggests`, but its RAPIDS runtime is a large, separate download
and is not present on most machines (including CRAN check machines). We guard
against both the package and the runtime being absent. When it is unavailable the
comparison code below is still shown, just not executed, and the rest of the
vignette is unaffected.

```{r backend-guard}
HAS_CUML <- requireNamespace("cuda.ml", quietly = TRUE)
if (HAS_CUML) {
  info <- tryCatch(cuda.ml::cuda_ml_backend_info(), error = function(e) NULL)
  HAS_CUML <- !is.null(info) && isTRUE(info$runtime_installed)
}
if (!HAS_CUML) {
  message("cuda.ml GPU runtime not available: the third-party comparison ",
          "is shown as code but not executed.")
}
HAS_CUML
```

### The oracle and our GPU fit

Both solve the same objective
`F(beta) = 1/(2n) ||y - X beta||^2 + lambda ||beta||_1` with no intercept and
no standardization. These two always run: the compiled path falls back to the
CPU reference shim when no CUDA backend was linked, so this works even on a
machine without a GPU.

```{r our-fit}
set.seed(42)
n <- 200L
p <- 20L
X <- matrix(rnorm(n * p), n, p)
beta_true <- c(2.5, -1.5, rep(0, p - 2L))
y <- drop(X %*% beta_true) + rnorm(n, sd = 0.4)
lambda <- 0.05

# one common objective, evaluated on any coefficient vector
objective <- function(b) {
  sum((y - drop(X %*% b))^2) / (2 * n) + lambda * sum(abs(b))
}

oracle <- lasso_fista_cpu(X, y, lambda = lambda)   # pure R
fit    <- cuda_lasso(X, y, lambda = lambda)       # rcupp (GPU or CPU shim)

cat(sprintf("backend                   : %s\n", fit$backend))
cat(sprintf("max |cuda_lasso - oracle| : %.3e\n",
            max(abs(fit$coefficients - oracle$coefficients))))
```

`lasso_fista_cpu()` and the compiled path share the numerical contract
line-for-line (deterministic power iteration for `L`, the same FISTA momentum
and soft-threshold), so the difference above is ~0 by construction.

### Against `cuda.ml` (RAPIDS cuML)

`cuda_ml_lasso.matrix()` fits lasso by **coordinate descent**, not FISTA, and
uses cuML's own stopping rule and normalization. We therefore do **not** expect
bit-identical coefficients; the meaningful checks are the common objective, the
sparsity pattern, and the correlation of the coefficient vectors.

To make the comparison fair we align the knobs with our model: `alpha = lambda`
(cuda.ml documents its `alpha` as comparable to glmnet's `lambda`),
`fit_intercept = FALSE`, a tight `tol`, and a large `max_iter`. Coefficients are
read from `model$xptr$coef`, the same field `cuda_ml_get_state()` exposes.

```{r cuml-compare, eval = HAS_CUML}
cuml <- cuda.ml::cuda_ml_lasso(
  X, y,
  alpha         = lambda,
  max_iter      = 10000L,
  tol           = 1e-8,
  fit_intercept = FALSE,
  selection     = "cyclic"
)
b_cuml <- as.numeric(cuml$xptr$coef)

knitr::kable(
  data.frame(
    method = c("lasso_fista_cpu (oracle)", "cuda_lasso (FISTA / GPU)",
               "cuda_ml_lasso (cuML / CD)"),
    objective = c(objective(oracle$coefficients),
                  objective(fit$coefficients),
                  objective(b_cuml)),
    nonzero = c(sum(abs(oracle$coefficients) > 1e-6),
                sum(abs(fit$coefficients) > 1e-6),
                sum(abs(b_cuml) > 1e-6))
  ),
  digits = 8,
  caption = "One objective, evaluated on all three coefficient vectors."
)
cat(sprintf("max |cuML - oracle| : %.3e\n",
            max(abs(b_cuml - oracle$coefficients))))
cat(sprintf("cor(cuML, oracle)   : %.6f\n",
            cor(b_cuml, oracle$coefficients)))
```

Interpretation: the three objectives should agree to the solver tolerances, the
non-zero count should match (the two planted signals, 2 of 20), and the
correlation should be ~1. Small coefficient differences are expected because
coordinate descent and FISTA approach the optimum differently. Because cuML's
internal loss normalization is not identical to ours, we always re-evaluate the
*same* objective above rather than trusting each solver's reported loss.

#### Enabling the live comparison

On a Linux x86_64 host with glibc >= 2.28, an NVIDIA driver >= 580 and R >= 4.1
(per the `cuda.ml` DESCRIPTION):

```r
install.packages("cuda.ml")        # pure-R wrapper, no compilation
cuda.ml::cuda_ml_install()         # downloads the RAPIDS cuML runtime
cuda.ml::cuda_ml_backend_info()$runtime_installed   # should be TRUE
```

Then rebuild this vignette and the `cuml-compare` chunk runs for real.

## Part 2 - CUDA build-system: gputools vs rcupp

`gputools` 2.1.0 and `rcupp` implement the **same optional-CUDA pattern**. The
point of this section is to make that pattern explicit and to note where
`gputools` handles more platforms than `rcupp` currently does. Sources compared:
the CRAN tarballs `gputools_2.1.0` and `cuda.ml_0.4.0`; the generated
`gputools/src/Makevars` comes from `src/Makevars.in`, so that template and
`INSTALL` are what we quote.

### The shared skeleton

1. An install-time `configure` at the package root **never fails** when CUDA is
   absent.
2. It renders `src/Makevars` from `src/Makevars.in` by substituting `@VAR@`
   placeholders.
3. `Makevars` selects the GPU objects or a single fallback object via a
   column-0 `OBJECTS =` line, and adds an rpath to the toolkit libraries.
4. A generated `Makevars` is excluded from the source tarball via
   `.Rbuildignore`, and `cleanup` removes it after the build.
5. Windows does not run `configure`; a `Makevars.win` (or the default object
   list) builds the fallback only.

`gputools/src/Makevars.in`:

```make
PKG_CPPFLAGS = -I. @CUDA_CPPFLAGS@
PKG_LIBS = @CUDA_LIBS@
OBJECTS = @GPUTOOLS_OBJECTS@
```

`rcupp/src/Makevars.in` (the same three substitutions, plus nvcc handling):

```make
CXX_STD = CXX17
CUDA_HOME = @CUDA_HOME@
NVCC = @NVCC@
NVCCFLAGS = @NVCCFLAGS@
PKG_CPPFLAGS = @CUDA_CPPFLAGS@
PKG_LIBS = @CUDA_LIBS@
OBJECTS = RcppExports.o rcupp_exports.o @EXTRA_OBJECTS@
%.o: %.cu
	$(NVCC) $(NVCCFLAGS) -c $< -o $@
```

`gputools/src/Makevars.win` is the explicit Windows fallback:

```make
# Windows does not run configure, and gputools has no Windows CUDA build:
# build only the fallback, whose GPU functions explain that.
OBJECTS = nocuda.o
```

### Side-by-side

| Aspect | gputools 2.1.0 | rcupp |
|---|---|---|
| `configure` source | autoconf: `configure.ac` -> generated 127 KB `configure` | hand-written ~80-line POSIX `sh` |
| Rendering | `AC_CONFIG_FILES([src/Makevars src/nocuda-reason.h])` | `sed ... src/Makevars.in > src/Makevars` |
| Fallback object | `nocuda.o` (GPU functions stop with an explanatory error) | `cpu_stub.o` (same C ABI, a CPU numerical oracle) |
| Detection order | `--with-cuda-include` / `--with-cuda-lib`, `--with-cuda-home`, `CUDA_HOME`, `CUDA_PATH`, dir above `nvcc`, `/usr/local/cuda` | `--with-cuda-home`, `CUDA_HOME`, `CUDA_PATH`, `nvcc` on PATH, `/usr/local/cuda` |
| Toolkit validation | `AC_CHECK_HEADERS` (cuda.h, cuda_runtime.h, nvrtc.h, cublas_v2.h, cusolverDn.h), `AC_SEARCH_LIBS` (cudart, nvrtc, cublas, cusolver), `CUDART_VERSION >= 11070` | file checks: executable `nvcc`, `cuda_runtime.h`, `libcudart.so*` |
| Conda layout | `targets/<arch>/include`, `lib/`, `targets/*/lib` | not handled (toolkit `include/`, `lib64/` only) |
| Compiled objects | every `src/*.cpp` except `nocuda.cpp` | fixed operator objects: `gpu_ops.o`, `lasso_fista_cuda.o` |
| GPU architecture | NVRTC compiles `inst/cuda/*.cu` at **runtime** for the current GPU (first call slower) | `nvcc -gencode arch=compute_89,code=sm_89` at **install** time (`RCUPP_CUDA_ARCH` overrides) |
| Windows | `src/Makevars.win` -> `nocuda.o`; recommends WSL2 | no `configure` -> CPU shim; CUDA needs WSL2 |
| Link flags | `-Wl,-rpath,${cuda_lib} ${LIBS}` | `-Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_LIBDIR -lcudart -lcublas` |
| `cleanup` | removes `*.o *.so Makevars config.log config.status autom4te.cache nocuda-reason.h` | removes `src/Makevars` |

### Multi-platform lessons from `gputools/INSTALL`

`gputools/INSTALL` spells out the portability story that both packages share:
the package "installs and loads without" a toolkit, reports `"installed WITHOUT
CUDA"` loudly when `configure` cannot find one, and simply errors inside GPU
functions at run time. Its detection order matches `rcupp`'s, with two extra
capabilities worth adopting:

- **Split include/lib overrides and conda layouts.** `--with-cuda-include` /
  `--with-cuda-lib`, and `CUDA_HOME=$CONDA_PREFIX` with
  `targets/<arch>/include` + `lib/`, cover conda and non-standard installs.
  `rcupp` currently assumes a single toolkit root with `include/` and `lib64/`.
- **Real probes instead of file existence.** `AC_CHECK_HEADERS`,
  `AC_SEARCH_LIBS` and the `CUDART_VERSION` compile test catch a partial or
  too-old toolkit that would otherwise fail at link time; `rcupp` only checks
  that a few files exist.

`gputools` also documents the two platform facts that matter here: Windows has
no native CUDA build (use WSL2, which is exactly how this project's GPU build
runs), and NVRTC runtime compilation avoids baking a single GPU architecture
into the binary. `rcupp` deliberately differs on both: as a *fixed* GPU operator
library it compiles its small `.cu` set statically with `nvcc` at install time
(no NVRTC, no first-call cost), and exposes `RCUPP_CUDA_ARCH` as the escape
hatch for other cards. Adding a `Makevars.win`, conda-layout probing, and
per-architecture `gencode` lists are the natural next steps if `rcupp` grows
beyond a single workstation.

### Takeaway

The "detect CUDA, render `Makevars`, keep a CPU fallback, never fail the
install" pattern is not ad hoc - it is the same one `gputools` ships on CRAN.
`rcupp` is a deliberately smaller instance of it: a fixed operator ABI, a
numerical-oracle fallback rather than a stub, and static `nvcc` compilation.
That makes the two-layer `rcupp` + `cudaGlmnet` design installable and
`R CMD check`-clean on any machine, while still linking the real GPU backend
where a toolkit and an NVIDIA GPU are present.
